items.title: Stock market correction? Whatever — Wall Street is bullish on 2027, and one chief investment officer sees the S&P 500 soaring 45% to 10,000
items.summary:
The Dow Jones Industrial Average and the S&P 500 joined the Nasdaq in correction territory as AI stocks plunged further, but 2026 is also winding down, and Wall Street is already putting out predictions for 2027.

Analysts see solid gains ahead, with the U.S. economy expected to continue chugging along on the back of massive hyperscaler spending and resilient consumers. Some also welcomed the recent decline for taking froth off markets that might otherwise start looking overheated.

Even this week’s selloff, which marked the worst weekly loss since the early days of the COVID-19 pandemic, was largely dismissed as a move driven more by emotion than fundamentals. 

“This does not mean stampedes are uninformative or palpitations never presage heart attacks, but today’s panic does not feel like an AI bust,” Viktor Shvets, head of global desk strategy at Macquarie Capital, said in a note Friday.

Michael Monaghan, portfolio manager and partner at Founder ETFs, quipped that the market is “selling first and asking questions later.” And Jamie Cox, managing partner for Harris Financial Group, predicted investors will “return to rationality” and look instead to consumption-boosting GDP. 

Meanwhile, Morgan Stanley chief U.S. equity strategist Michael Wilson said earlier this week that the S&P 500 would finish 2027 at 8,700, representing a 26% jump from current levels and a 15% rally when he made the call.

“We see the mid-cycle transition now ending with a more stable mid-cycle backdrop evolving in 2027,” he wrote.

Goldman Sachs also sees the broad market index soaring to 8,700…
items.t: Stock market correction? Whatever — Wall Street is bullish on 2027, and one chief investment officer sees the S&P 500 soaring 45% to 10,000

items.title: The AI bust is a growing threat to China’s economy and a ‘moment of real danger’ for President Xi Jinping, analyst warns
items.summary:
U.S. investors are facing a meltdown in tech stocks and the possible end of the AI boom, but the bubble has already popped in China, where an even worse market crash threatens the economy and President Xi Jinping, according to Yardeni Research.

China’s tech-heavy STAR 50 index has tumbled 44% from its high this summer, while the Nasdaq is down 18% from its record—even after U.S. stocks suffered their worst week since the early days of the COVID-19 pandemic.

That’s thrown a wrench into Xi’s plans for the economy, Yardeni said in a note earlier this month. While the Chinese leader was riding high as host to global leaders this week, the market’s downturn jeopardizes his plan to turn China’s savers into stock investors who can finance the AI buildout and de-emphasize the property market.

Real estate accounts for roughly 70% of household wealth in China and was traditionally a place to stash savings. But the housing crash has weighed on consumer demand, even producing intermittent deflation. Business investment is also falling, with October data showing property investment sank nearly 22%.

With the domestic market still weak, Beijing has instead relied on a flood of cheap exports to keep the economy growing while also deploying the “national team” of state-backed banks to pump money into the stock market.

But according to Yardeni, Chinese stocks collapsed this year due in part to cutthroat competition, heavier tax burdens, higher energy costs, tariffs, and the risk that China’s trading partners will block exports being sold at ultra-low prices.

“To keep AI funding…
items.t: The AI bust is a growing threat to China’s economy and a ‘moment of real danger’ for President Xi Jinping, analyst warns

items.title: Even FEMA officials are worried about the string of outages and withdrew extra cash — ‘This is scary, and there is no leadership’
items.summary:
The Trump administration has insisted that the recent surge in network outages isn’t due to a cyberattack, but those responsible for the federal government’s emergency response aren’t so sure.

Two officials at the Federal Emergency Management Agency told the Washington Post they were concerned about the outages and were having trouble believing they were a coincidence.

One official took out extra cash, and the other reported being bombarded with questions from former classmates asking whether they should prepare for an emergency.

“There is nothing on this scale that has happened before in this many sectors this close together,” one of the officials told the Post . “This is scary, and there is no leadership.”

FEMA didn’t respond to a request for comment.

Even before everything appeared to break down, Americans were already on edge after the  Pentagon launched an initiative called FORTRESS , which seeks to ensure that every major U.S. military base can run for 90 days without outside help if a war cuts off power and supply chains.

Then came a month of cyberattacks that hit hundreds of companies and institutions around the world. The hacking spree was so widespread that it was dubbed “Black October.” The Nvidia spy scandal also didn’t help sentiment.

Last Thursday, Microsoft’s email and other office tools went down. Last Friday, the Federal Aviation Administration grounded all planes for more than four hours. It later blamed a copper wire that was being upgraded to a fiber-optic cable.

Days later, companies like Chase,  Wells Fargo ,  United Airlines , and Apple saw…
items.t: Even FEMA officials are worried about the string of outages and withdrew extra cash — ‘This is scary, and there is no leadership’

items.title: ‘This seems like an extreme privacy violation.’ Surprising messages from the Muse AI agent are unnerving Meta’s own employees, report says
items.summary:
Meta employees have raised concerns about the company’s Muse AI agent after receiving unprompted notifications that tapped into private information, according to internal posts seen by Reuters .

In one example, a Meta staffer reported that Muse sent her a reminder on her personal phone to respond to a message from her sister on the encrypted messaging service Signal.

“This seems like an extreme privacy violation. I definitely did not grant it access to other apps, or recall being asked about this,” the employee posted.

A Meta colleague also shared that he got unsolicited chats related to apps he had not connected and discovered Muse was set up by default with permission to access push notifications on Android phones, Reuters reported.

Another employee posted that during his chats about fishing-related weather and tide information, Muse said, “BTW, two bank updates, your Capital One balance is $2722.58, your Charles Schwab balance is $5899.57.”

Other random Muse messages also took Meta workers aback, including a question about parental control over access to their child’s data and a conversation about picking up a coffee table that raised concern over “possible cross-account context leak.”

In response to the internal posts about Muse, a member of Meta’s Superintelligence team said the agent appeared to be hallucinating due to built-in prompts that were designed to engage users between sessions, according to Reuters.

“These (hallucinations) unfortunately bias towards the most uncomfortable topics, like finances/security/safety, which sucks,” he said, adding that other…
items.t: ‘This seems like an extreme privacy violation.’ Surprising messages from the Muse AI agent are unnerving Meta’s own employees, report says

items.title: The $120,500 cost of being ‘Sister’: SNL sketch puts a face on America’s caregiving crisis
items.summary:
On the Nov. 14 episode of Saturday Night Live , host John Mulaney starred in a parody drug ad for “Sister,” “a live-in, 24/7 elder care provider that is completely free and also your sister.”

The sketch spread across social media within days, largely because so many viewers saw their own families in it. Its jokes land on real pressure points in American caregiving: who does the work, what it costs them, and how much more of it is coming.

63 million Americans now provide ongoing care 

A 2025 report from AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving found that 63 million Americans, nearly 1 in 4 adults, had provided ongoing care in the past year to an adult or child with a medical condition or disability. That is 45% more caregivers than a decade earlier.

The work has also gotten harder. More than 40% of caregivers provide high-intensity care, and more than half perform medical and nursing tasks such as giving injections and managing catheters. Only 22% have been trained to do them.

An aging population is the main driver, says Geoff Gross, founder and CEO of Medical Guardian, a Philadelphia-based medical alert and connected-care company. But strains on the broader care system are pushing more Americans into the role.

“What we’re also seeing is pressures on in-home care and labor overall,” Gross said. “There’s a burden on caregivers right now that is not scalable.”

Paid help is scarce and expensive. As gerontologists Jane Tavares and Marc Cohen wrote for Fortune , a home health aide runs a median of about $6,688 a month, while the direct care workforce remains…
items.t: The $120,500 cost of being ‘Sister’: SNL sketch puts a face on America’s caregiving crisis

items.title: ‘An extraordinary and extreme backstop’: Earthjustice warns Army off bypassing paused Iowa permit
items.summary:
A federal appeals court has paused the emergency permit authorizing the U.S. Army to blow up nearly five tons of degraded lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa. But the Justice Department told the court Friday that the Army may be able to proceed without it.

In a notice filed on behalf of the Environmental Protection Agency, government lawyers said they would oppose a motion by two environmental groups to keep the permit on hold. The notice added that “in qualifying emergency situations,” EPA regulations authorize the Army, which is not a party to the case, “to implement waste treatment activity without an EPA permit” when there is “an immediate threat to human health, public safety, property, or the environment.”

The notice did not say whether the Army plans to go ahead with the detonation, now set for Monday, Nov. 23. An Army Sustainment Command spokesperson did not respond Friday when asked whether the Army would proceed while the stay is in place, the Iowa Capital Dispatch reported . On Friday evening, Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds activated the State Emergency Operations Center to coordinate state, federal, and local agencies ahead of the planned blast.

Thien Chau, a senior attorney at Earthjustice, which represents the groups, called the emergency provision “an extraordinary and extreme backstop” and said the groups “strongly urge” the Army not to rely on it.

The standoff leaves residents of southeastern Iowa and western Illinois facing a weekend of uncertainty over whether a plume of lead-laden dust will drift across their towns and farmland…
items.t: ‘An extraordinary and extreme backstop’: Earthjustice warns Army off bypassing paused Iowa permit

items.title: Only 18% of Gen Z workers want to build AI skills. A Wharton professor says using AI is riskier for them
items.summary:
The generation with the longest careers ahead of them appears to be the least interested in sharpening their AI skills, according to research from talent services firm Seramount released Thursday: Only 18% of Gen Z employees want to develop or improve their AI skills, compared with 36% of millennials, 46% of Gen Xers, and 43% of baby boomers.

For younger workers, using AI could come with a different set of professional risks than it does for their more experienced colleagues.

“Because younger workers haven’t had the same amount of time in their career fields to build up their standing as experts, using a technology that blurs their own contribution to their work can feel especially risky,” Jessica Reif, an assistant professor of management at the University of Pennsylvania’s Wharton School, told Fortune .

The survey of more than 1,800 U.S. white-collar employees at companies with at least 500 workers, conducted in June through NORC’s AmeriSpeak panel, found that 58% of Gen Z employees use AI in their current roles, compared with 60% of baby boomers, 63% of millennials, and 67% of Gen Xers. Seramount defined Gen Z as workers 29 and younger.

That leaves a puzzle. Gen Z workers, often cast as digital natives, use AI at nearly the same rate as baby boomers but show far less interest in getting better at it.

Younger workers worry AI makes them look less capable 

Younger workers are considerably more concerned about what using AI might say about their own abilities.

Some 22% of Gen Z employees surveyed by Seramount worry that using AI could lead others to question their…
items.t: Only 18% of Gen Z workers want to build AI skills. A Wharton professor says using AI is riskier for them

items.title: Goldman Sachs admits the ‘AI unwind’ has spiraled into something more dangerous — and it’s watching for 3 signs of bottom
items.summary:
The S&P 500 closed Friday in a correction, falling 3.59% to 6,918.45 for its seventh straight loss and its longest losing streak since February 2020. The Nasdaq Composite dropped 5.28% and is now down more than 2% for the year . Goldman Sachs notes the index is 12% below its Oct. 6 record, and its strategists have named the three things they’d need to see before calling a bottom.

Snider’s note said the sell-off “expanded this week from an AI unwind to a broader growth downgrade,” noting that the S&P 500 excluding AI had held up until this week and is now 6% below its high. Goldman’s AI stock basket is down 32% since Oct. 6. Cyclical stocks have lagged defensives by 5 percentage points over the past 10 days.

Goldman’s note was written before Friday’s rout was fully in its data. Its exhibits are priced as of Nov. 19 and its hedge fund data run through that date. So the question is whether Friday supplied what the note was looking for — the situation could be even worse in markets than it acknowledged.

The three conditions 

Goldman said any one of the following would support a bottom and a recovery: news that raises confidence in AI earnings, a dovish Fed signal, or a big drop in investor positioning.

Condition 1: AI earnings. This is the one the market is trying to test. Investor Dan Niles told CNBC that a price war between Anthropic and OpenAI is hurting both, noting their combined sequential revenue growth fell from 75% in the second quarter to 48% in the third, while combined losses rose from $7.9 billion to about $8.4 billion. Reuters cited a valuation of about 40…
items.t: Goldman Sachs admits the ‘AI unwind’ has spiraled into something more dangerous — and it’s watching for 3 signs of bottom

items.title: Goodwill CEO says hiring managers are going behind their bosses’ backs and looking for workers with college degrees, not skills
items.summary:
More bad news for job seekers—especially non-grad Gen Zers. Just because an employer claims it’s ditching degree requirements to recruit more diverse talent, that doesn’t mean its hiring managers are actually doing it. 

When major employers like Google , Microsoft , IBM , and Apple all eliminated their long-held degree requirements for jobs , other firms rushed to follow their example. But that promise may be limited to their job ads. 

Goodwill’s CEO Steve Preston told Fortune that while most CEOs have good intentions, they can’t control every interview or job offer. And so the promise of skills-first hiring may not be reaching the millions of jobless Gen Zers who need it.

“Right now, employers are consistently saying they want to hire for skills, not necessarily degrees,” Preston said. “But the proof is in the pudding. Not everybody does it.” 

He added: “What I hear from a lot of people is, ‘Yeah, the top says we need to do this,’ but when it gets to the hiring professionals, it doesn’t always trickle down.”

The charity has more than 650 job centers and saw nearly 2 million people use its employment services last year, and Preston said he’s preparing for an influx of jobless Gen Zers thanks to automation .

Gen Zers without degrees are struggling most with unemployment 

While the opportunities for young people without degrees are certainly growing, Preston says they’re ultimately still more likely to face unemployment than Gen Zers with a degree. 

“What I’m seeing is, of the overall unemployment, people without college degrees have no jobs,” the 66-year-old CEO,…
items.t: Goodwill CEO says hiring managers are going behind their bosses’ backs and looking for workers with college degrees, not skills

items.title: Data centers full of U.S. chips are serving Chinese AI models–undermining Trump’s tech ambitions
items.summary:
The Nvidia-Megaspeed saga has drawn attention to a significant gap in U.S. export controls: Chinese companies remotely accessing AI chips located outside of China. On Monday, largely in response to the scandal, the U.S. Commerce Department issued a rule closing this loophole.

But while this long-overdue action can help U.S. AI labs widen the gap between their models and those of their Chinese competitors, there’s still a paradox at the heart of Washington’s AI strategy: the U.S. infrastructure spreading around the world is helping Chinese models gain traction.

The Trump administration wants the U.S. to dominate AI from chips to models. Key to the president’s vision is exporting high-end, U.S.-designed chips to countries around the world. Increasingly, these chips—designed by companies like Nvidia—are being deployed in data centers in Latin America, the Middle East, and Southeast Asia.

But U.S. leadership in compute infrastructure doesn’t just help U.S. AI model developers. It helps their Chinese competitors too.

Today, U.S.-owned data centers filled with U.S. chips still rent capacity out to inference providers, which use that capability to serve Chinese large language models (LLMs) to global users.

Chinese models are running on U.S. chips, and the U.S. AI infrastructure build-out is counterintuitively helping Chinese model developers compete. This poses a problem for U.S. AI preeminence, which will need global consumers and enterprises to choose U.S.-developed LLMs over Chinese ones.

The contradiction at the heart of the Trump administration’s dreams of AI dominance…
items.t: Data centers full of U.S. chips are serving Chinese AI models–undermining Trump’s tech ambitions

items.title: ‘The doom of humanity’: will the quest to make robotic hands render us obsolete?
items.summary:
The one thing stopping AI taking over the world – or at least everyone’s jobs? Dexterity. Human hands are anatomical marvels that engineers have struggled for years to replicate. Experts are racing to change that

Just outside Luton, in an Amazon warehouse the size of four football pitches, yellow shelving units pirouette in a digitally choreographed dance. Tubs containing a Lego Spider-Man kit, followed by dishwasher tablets, followed by a pouch of muscle building protein powder whiz along conveyor belts, until they arrive at a human being tasked with stacking the shelving unit that has come to a stop in front of their workstation. This, Amazon says, is the “symphony of people and technology” to which the retail giant owes its success.

Following a barrage of negative publicity about working practices, Amazon began to open up its fulfilment centres to carefully controlled free public tours a decade ago. items.title: Forget rogue robots, it’s tech billionaires and AI cricket that should really terrify us | Barney Ronay
items.summary:
The encroachment of artificial intelligence smells like the death of sport. Can we find the will and collective backbone to resist?

There was an interesting development this week in the endless rolling mega-froth over tech billionaire Jensen Huang, a saga that may or may not have involved some kind of adulterous 63-year-old honey trap spy dynamic.

The latest suggestion being punted about is that, whatever his raw human frailties, Huang is in fact “irreplaceable” as the president of Nvidia. Only this guy can do it. Only this leather-jacketed human visionary, who looks in every available photo like your GCSE chemistry teacher’s profile pic on TerrifiedUkrainianSinglesWantToDateYou.com, can manage this key artificial intelligence mission.

items.t: Forget rogue robots, it’s tech billionaires and AI cricket that should really terrify us | Barney Ronay

items.title: The Guardian view on Britain and Europe: Burnham’s reset cannot be the final destination | Editorial
items.summary:
It’s welcome news that Labour has reopened doors that the Conservatives slammed shut. But the fundamental dilemma over European integration remains

Andy Burnham on Friday announced a long-awaited deal to ease some of Brexit’s barriers. But EU sources say the agreements, or at least some of them, won’t take effect until Britain has resolved a dispute over its demand for European students to pay the same university tuition fees as British ones. The prime minister had hoped to turn the page on Brexit’s endless haggling. Instead, he was reminded that closer ties come at a price. This does not negate his achievement. The deals ease trade barriers on food, shield British exporters from EU carbon tariffs and let up to 100,000 young people on each side live and work across the Channel for three years. But Mr Burnham cannot claim an unqualified diplomatic victory.

Clearly, such an advance would have been unimaginable under the Conservatives or Reform. The Tories say they will rip up the agreements, though that stance carries the risk of alienating voters lost to the Liberal Democrats in 2024. Nigel Farage

items.title: AI is imposing a hidden ‘cognitive tax’ on the lowest-paid workers
items.summary:
It’s time to rethink welfare as AI reshapes the economy and wears down the brains of some of the most vulnerable workers

AI is adding to the cognitive load of workers already stretched thin by unpredictable pay, insecure housing and mounting debt – and the lowest paid feel it most. We need to rethink welfare for an economy being reshaped by AI.

Throughout the history of the study of economics, the human brain, which directs our labour, judgment and resilience, has rarely been considered an asset in its own right. The emerging AI economy is changing that. As machines take on routine work, what becomes most valuable is the judgment, creativity and insights only people can provide. Economists coined a term for this in recent years: brain capital.

Professor Dame Henrietta Moore is founder and director of the UCL Institute for Global Prosperity and co-leads The New Alignment, the institute’s G20 policy programme

items.t: AI is imposing a hidden ‘cognitive tax’ on the lowest-paid workers

items.title: Don’t blame cyber-attacks for recent outages. The real villain is the US economy | Bruce Schneier
items.summary:
Our tech infrastructure is riddled with problems. But they’re all downstream of the incentives baked into shareholder capitalism

It’s been a bad week for our computerized infrastructure. We’ve seen outages at Microsoft, the FAA, a handful of banks, United Airlines, an unnamed classified NSA network, and Apple. People should be forgiven for suspecting a coordinated cyber-attack, a common cause, or at least a conspiracy. But there is none.

The incidents are unrelated. They’re not the result of any cyber-attack, coordinated or not. And, even more surprising, they don’t seem to be the result of AI. (We can’t say anything about the NSA; we’ll probably never know the details of that one.) It’s really just a series of unfortunate coincidences.

Continue reading...
items.t: Don’t blame cyber-attacks for recent outages. The real villain is the US economy | Bruce Schneier
